DEATH-ON-PROPERTY AND HIV/AIDS-STATUS DISCLOSURE ('STIGMATIZED PROPERTY,' CIV. CODE § 1710.2) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Civil Code Section 1710.2, the statute addressing whether an owner of real property or an agent must disclose to a prospective transferee that an occupant died on the property, the manner of that death, or that an occupant had HIV/AIDS, as it may apply to the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. It states what the statute's own text provides, including the conditions under which it says no disclosure duty exists. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular disclosure, and it does not tell either Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any specific death or health-status fact concerning the property.

NO DUTY TO DISCLOSE A DEATH OR ITS MANNER AFTER THREE YEARS
Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, subject to a stated exception for intentional misrepresentation, an owner of real property or the owner's agent, and any agent of a transferee, is not required to disclose to the transferee the occurrence of an occupant's death upon the property, or the manner of that death, where the death occurred more than three years before the date the transferee offers to purchase, lease, or rent the property; the statute states that this is because such a fact is not a material fact requiring disclosure. The statute further states that no cause of action arises against an owner, the owner's agent, or a transferee's agent for not disclosing this fact. The statute's own definition of "transferee" for this purpose includes a purchaser, a lessee, and a renter of real property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) (1) Subject to subdivision (d), an owner of real property or his or her agent, or any agent of a transferee of real property, is not required to disclose either of the following to the transferee, as these are not material facts that require disclosure:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(1), California Civil Code, scope of the no-duty-to-disclose rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  "(A) The occurrence of an occupant’s death upon the real property or the manner of death where the death has occurred more than three years prior to the date the transferee offers to purchase, lease, or rent the real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(1)(A), California Civil Code, the death/manner-of-death rule and three-year period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  "(3) No cause of action shall arise against an owner or his or her agent or any agent of a transferee for not disclosing facts pursuant to paragraph (1)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(3), California Civil Code, no cause of action for not disclosing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  "(B) “Transferee” includes a purchaser, lessee, or renter of real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(2)(B), California Civil Code, statutory definition of "transferee" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text states the non-disclosure rule using the single, undifferentiated phrase "the manner of death" — it does not itself break "manner of death" into categories such as natural, accidental, suicide, or homicide, and it does not state a different rule for any one category; this document does not add a categorization the statute's own text does not contain. The three-year period runs from "the date the transferee offers to purchase, lease, or rent the real property," a specific triggering event stated in the statute itself — this document does not calculate or apply that date to any specific transaction. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines a death-on-property disclosure duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property transfer; other states' stigmatized-property rules, including any lookback period, vary and some states impose no such statute at all. The no-cause-of-action language is part of the same statutory subdivision (a) as the core disclosure rule and is not an independent corroborating source for it.

NO DUTY TO DISCLOSE AN OCCUPANT'S HIV/AIDS STATUS
Separately from the death-and-manner-of-death rule, Civil Code Section 1710.2 states that an owner of real property or the owner's agent, and any agent of a transferee, is not required to disclose to the transferee that an occupant of the property was living with HIV or died from AIDS-related complications; the statute states this is because that fact, too, is not a material fact requiring disclosure. Unlike the death/manner-of-death rule, the statute's own text attaches no three-year (or other) time limit to this HIV/AIDS-status rule. The statute also states that it is the intent of the California Legislature to occupy the field of regulation of disclosure concerning the HIV-positive status of a prior occupant in situations affecting the transfer of real property or any estate or interest in real property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(B) That an occupant of that property was living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or died from AIDS-related complications."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(1)(B), California Civil Code, the HIV/AIDS-status no-duty rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  "(b) It is the intent of the Legislature to occupy the field of regulation of disclosure related to either of the following: (1) Deaths occurring upon real property. (2) The HIV-positive status of a prior occupant in situations affecting the transfer of real property or any estate or interest in real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(b), California Civil Code, legislative intent to occupy the field (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  Known gap: "Occupy the field" is the statute's own characterization of its relationship to other disclosure regulation on this specific subject; this document does not interpret what that phrase does or does not preempt for any particular local ordinance, regulation, or common-law claim, and does not resolve whether or how it interacts with disclosure duties arising under a different statute. The statute's own text pairs this occupy-the-field statement with deaths occurring upon real property as well, in the same subdivision (b); this clause focuses on the HIV/AIDS-status half of that statement, and the death-related half is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction treats disclosure of a prior occupant's HIV/AIDS status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property transfer.

WHAT THE NO-DUTY RULES DO NOT CHANGE
Civil Code Section 1710.2 states two express limits on its own no-duty rules. First, the statute states that it does not alter the law relating to disclosure of any other physical or mental condition or disease, and does not relieve an owner or agent of any obligation to disclose the physical condition of the premises. Second, the statute states that it does not immunize an owner or the owner's agent from making an intentional misrepresentation in response to a direct inquiry from a transferee, or a prospective transferee, concerning deaths on the property; the statute's core no-duty rule is itself stated as subject to this misrepresentation limitation. The statute defines "agent," for purposes of the entire section, to include any person licensed under the California real estate licensing law referenced in the statute's own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) This section shall not be construed to alter the law relating to disclosure pertaining to any other physical or mental condition or disease, and this section shall not relieve any owner or agent of any obligation to disclose the physical condition of the premises."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(c), California Civil Code, no effect on other physical-condition disclosure duties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  "(d) This section shall not be construed to immunize an owner or his or her agent from making an intentional misrepresentation in response to a direct inquiry from a transferee or a prospective transferee of real property, concerning deaths on the real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(d), California Civil Code, intentional-misrepresentation carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  "(A) “Agent” includes any person licensed pursuant to Part 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(2)(A), California Civil Code, statutory definition of "agent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1710.2.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text addresses only an "intentional misrepresentation in response to a direct inquiry" — it does not, in this text, define what qualifies as an intentional misrepresentation or a direct inquiry, and this document does not resolve either question for any specific exchange. The "other physical or mental condition or disease" limitation and the intentional-misrepresentation limitation are each stated in a separate subdivision of the same statutory section — subdivisions (c) and (d) respectively — and are not corroborating sources for one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction bounds its own stigmatized-property disclosure exemption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property transfer.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding death-on-property and HIV/AIDS-status disclosure under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, concerning the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific disclosure question concerning this property.
